title: Combining forces to reveal the faintest objects in our Universe
caption: The Milky Way above an Auxiliary Telescope of the VLT, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: The purple, dusty band of the Milky Way stretches high above one of the Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory. Each of these telescopes has a mirror 1.8 metres across.
The Auxiliary Telescopes can also work with the larger Unit Telescopes, and together they form a giant interferometer, the ESO Very Large Telescope Interferometer.

An interferometer combines the light collected by several telescopes spread apart from one another. The combined system can pick out much finer detail than any single one of its telescopes. According to ESO, this arrangement reveals details up to 25 times finer than any one of the telescopes could manage alone. It is a way of building the sharpness of a very large telescope out of several smaller ones working in concert.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure collects much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more colourful than it would to someone standing there.

explore: The Milky Way overhead is our own galaxy seen from inside its disc, where dust lanes break up the glow of countless distant stars.
